clue.text: Noble order whereby may hang a jewel

parts.note: an earl is a nobleman, a British peer
the OBE is the Order of the British Empire, a British honour

explanation.surface: A grand aristocratic decoration from which a gem might dangle.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a jewel hanging from a medal; the jewel really hangs from part of the head.
explanation.definitionFit: Earrings, jewels included, are hung through the soft lower part of the outer ear.

clue.text: A plimsoll 12 that helps establish connections

parts.note: a dap is a dialect word, chiefly Welsh and West Country, for a plimsoll or canvas sports shoe
the answer to clue 12, a rocky Dartmoor hill

explanation.surface: A sports shoe and a hill somehow form a device for linking things up.
explanation.walkthrough: '12' points to the answer at 12-across, TOR. A plimsoll is a light canvas gym shoe.
explanation.definitionFit: An adaptor is a fitting that lets plugs or parts of differing kinds be joined together.

clue.text: Mad women go to law over right to garden equipment

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: mad suggests the letters of women going wild and rearranging

explanation.surface: Furious women sue over their right to some gardening kit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mad' is the anagram signal for the women; in this down clue 'over' simply means the legal word comes first, above the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A machine for cutting grass is a standard piece of a gardener's kit.

clue.text: Raillery (before in old railway)

indicators.note: in places the word for before within the abbreviation for the old railway

parts.note: BR was British Rail, the former UK state railway
ante is Latin for before, as in ante-room

explanation.surface: A bracketed note seemingly about something earlier on a defunct railway.
explanation.walkthrough: The old railway is British Rail, the UK's nationalised network until the 1990s; 'in' is the container signal. 'Raillery' teases with 'railway'.
explanation.definitionFit: Raillery is good-humoured teasing, the same playful exchange of jokes as banter.

clue.text: Struggle when article is gone without

parts.note: a is the indefinite article

indicators.note: without here means outside, so gone surrounds is

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone finds it hard when a newspaper piece has vanished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' has its old sense of outside, so the word gone surrounds is rather than lacking it.
explanation.definitionFit: To agonise is to wrestle mentally, struggling painfully over a decision.

clue.text: Sound egg curdled fish

indicators.note: curdled describes something broken up and changed, so the letters are mixed

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A good egg has gone off and turned into fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Gudgeons are small European freshwater fish of the carp family, often used as bait.

clue.text: Cry from mount in Near East

indicators.note: in places the abbreviation for East inside the word for near

parts.note: nigh is an old word for near
E is the compass abbreviation for East

explanation.surface: A call heard from a mountain somewhere in the Middle East.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mount' reads as a mountain but means a horse; 'Near East' looks like one place but splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A mount is a horse that is ridden, and the cry a horse makes is its whinny.

clue.text: Cunning with minimal sound

indicators.note: sound tells us to take a word as it is spoken rather than spelled

parts.note: slight means minimal or very small

explanation.surface: Craftiness that makes almost no noise.
explanation.definitionFit: Sleight is dexterous trickery or craft, as in sleight of hand.

clue.text: Like party leaders before an election?

definitions.text: Like party leaders before an election?

parts.words: Like party leaders before an election?
parts.note: politicians campaigning are striving to govern; the phrase is also industrial action where staff stick strictly to regulations

explanation.surface: A description of politicians in the run-up to polling day.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally the phrase means labouring in order to govern; its usual sense is a go-slow protest.
explanation.definitionFit: Candidates are toiling hard with the aim of holding power, a literal reading of the go-slow idiom.

clue.text: Naturalist has ladies' club in stitches

indicators.note: in puts the ladies' club inside the word for stitches

parts.note: to darn is to mend with stitches
the WI is the Women's Institute, a British women's organisation

explanation.surface: A nature scientist visits a women's group and has everyone laughing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In stitches' suggests helpless laughter, but it is a container instruction. The WI, the Women's Institute, is a British club for women.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Darwin was the Victorian naturalist behind the theory of evolution.

clue.text: Hourglass likely to be pensioned off

definitions.meaning: an hourglass is an old-fashioned device for measuring time
a veteran, someone elderly and near retirement

explanation.surface: An antique sand clock fit for the scrapheap.
explanation.definitionFit: An elderly veteran is jokingly an aged clock, and an hourglass is a timer from long ago.

clue.text: Mostly wrong as High Willhays

indicators.note: mostly means most but not all of the word, dropping its final letter

parts.note: a tort is a civil wrong in law

explanation.surface: A claim that something is largely mistaken, likened to a place.
explanation.walkthrough: High Willhays is the highest point of Dartmoor, a moorland in Devon, England; such rocky Dartmoor hills are called tors.
explanation.definitionFit: High Willhays is an example of a rocky hilltop, the tallest on Dartmoor.

clue.text: Thwart the unknown in confused times

indicators.note: in puts the unknown quantity inside the jumbled letters
confused means mixed up, so the letters of times are rearranged

parts.note: Y is a standard algebraic unknown

explanation.surface: Mysterious, muddled times frustrate someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Confused' is the anagram signal and 'in' places the algebra unknown within the mixed letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To stymie someone is to obstruct or frustrate their plans, the same as thwarting them.

clue.text: A thousand and 7 over, eh? Not far off the ground

parts.note: K stands for a thousand, as in kilo

indicators.note: over means overturned or rearranged, so these letters are mixed

parts.note: the answer to clue 7, a horse's cry

explanation.surface: A cricket-like tally of a thousand and seven overs, met with a puzzled eh.
explanation.walkthrough: '7' points to the answer at 7-down, the horse's cry; 'over' is the anagram signal for it together with the interjection.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that reaches only up to a person's knee is low, close to floor level.

clue.text: Coaxed to start rising in early morning

indicators.note: in places the opening letter inside the word for daybreak

parts.note: dawn is the earliest part of the morning

indicators.note: start means the first letter of the next word

explanation.surface: Someone persuaded to get up at daybreak.
explanation.definitionFit: Drawn out or coaxed, as when a reluctant person is drawn into talking.

clue.text: Dressed in a tie, man found dead

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: dressed means arranged or prepared, signalling that the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A smartly attired corpse discovered in a tie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dressed' looks like clothing but signals the anagram of the three words after 'in', giving a word for living.
explanation.definitionFit: Inanimate means lifeless, without the spark of life, as a corpse is.

clue.text: Old economist keeping nothing at English distillery

indicators.note: keeping means holding inside, so the economist's name surrounds nothing

parts.note: Thomas Malthus was an English economist of the late 1700s
O is the figure zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A long-dead economist kept nothing at an English whisky works.
explanation.definitionFit: A building where barley is malted for brewing or distilling is loosely a distillery.

clue.text: Sculpture has to remain over sailor's about turn

indicators.note: over here means covering, so the word for remain sits around the rest

parts.note: to stay is to remain

indicators.note: about means around, so the sailor encloses the turn

parts.note: a tar is a sailor
U is a turn, as in a U-turn

explanation.surface: A sculpture must stay put while a sailor spins round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About turn' looks like a military order but splits: 'about' puts the sailor round a U-turn's letter, and 'over' sets the word for remain around that.
explanation.definitionFit: Statuary is the collective term for statues, that is sculpture.

clue.text: Exaggerate Putin's position?

definitions.meaning: to overplay or inflate a claim
as Russia's leader Putin is placed above, at the head of, the nation

explanation.surface: A query on whether the Russian leader's stance is overblown.
explanation.definitionFit: To exaggerate is to inflate a claim; read as two words, it also describes a leader sitting above the nation.

clue.text: House in which is a rogue

parts.note: a villa is a house
taken as written

explanation.surface: A house that a scoundrel lives in.
explanation.definitionFit: A villain is a wicked person, a scoundrel or rogue.

clue.text: Photograph collection nearly all posterior

indicators.note: nearly means not quite all of the word, losing its last letter

parts.note: the bum is British slang for the bottom or posterior

explanation.surface: A set of photos nearly all of people's backsides.
explanation.definitionFit: A book in which photographs are mounted and kept is the usual home for snaps.

clue.text: Association of states, lots about 50, which is gutless

parts.note: the UN is the United Nations

indicators.note: about means around, so the word for lots encloses fifty

parts.note: many means lots
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: An international body with dozens of members, described as cowardly.
explanation.definitionFit: Unmanly in old use means lacking courage, cowardly.

clue.text: Writer set about being confined

parts.note: a pen is a writing instrument

indicators.note: about here means turned round, so the word for set is read backwards

parts.note: to put is to set down

explanation.surface: An author starts work while locked up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' is the reversal signal for the word for set, which follows the writer.
explanation.definitionFit: Pent-up means held in or confined, like suppressed feelings.

clue.text: Leave poor 12 to give you a lift

indicators.note: poor suggests something badly formed, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the answer to clue 12, a rocky Dartmoor hill

explanation.surface: Leaving a hill in bad shape just to cheer you up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor' turns LEAVE into ELEVA; '12' is the answer at 12-across, TOR.
explanation.definitionFit: An elevator, a lift in British usage, carries people between floors.

clue.text: Film of culture almost devoid

indicators.note: culture here means cultivate or work over, signalling that the letters are reshaped
almost means the word loses its final letter

explanation.surface: A film said to be almost without any culture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' cuts DEVOID to DEVOI, and 'culture', read as cultivating, reworks those letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A video is a recorded film, especially on tape or disc.

clue.text: Dig up one-time philosopher

parts.note: ex means former or one-time
David Hume was an 18th-century Scottish philosopher

explanation.surface: Unearthing a former thinker.
explanation.definitionFit: To exhume is to dig a body out of its grave.

clue.text: Vessel in which to pour noggins

indicators.note: in signals letters sitting inside the next words

explanation.surface: A container for serving small drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: An urn is a large vessel for tea or a vase-like container.

clue.text: Hard nail bent to offer support

indicators.note: bent means twisted out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A tough nail gets bent while holding something up.
explanation.definitionFit: A rail fixed beside stairs is held for support.

clue.text: Not quite straight soldier failing to report for duty

indicators.note: not quite means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: true means straight, as in aligned
a soldier ant is a kind of ant

explanation.surface: A not entirely honest soldier skips duty.
explanation.definitionFit: A truant is one who stays away without permission, as from school or work.

clue.text: Man upset about Blair having contrary term

indicators.note: about means around, so the jumbled letters enclose the name
upset means knocked over and disordered, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: Tony Blair was UK Prime Minister 1997-2007

explanation.surface: A man annoyed with a former Prime Minister for using a word meaning the opposite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' is the anagram signal for man, and 'about' makes those mixed letters go round the former Prime Minister's first name.
explanation.definitionFit: An antonym is a word of opposite meaning, such as hot for cold.

clue.text: Kiwi more fitting with unknowns?

parts.note: apter means more apt, more fitting
Y and X are algebraic unknowns

explanation.surface: A New Zealander described as better suited to mysteries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kiwi' suggests a New Zealander, but it is the flightless bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The apteryx is the scientific genus name for the flightless New Zealand bird.
